newsitem.title: INDIA: India industry welcomes coNvertibility timetable.
newsitem.headline: India industry welcomes coNvertibility timetable.

text.p: Indian industrialists urged the government on Tuesday to implement the recommendations of an official report outlining the path to make the rupee fully convertible by the end of the century.

"A phased move towards full convertibility will infuse greater confidence among foreign investors," V. Raghuraman, secretary general of the Associated Chambers of Commerce and Industry (Assocham), told Reuters.
A committee appointed by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) submitted its recommendations, listing preconditions needed before the rupee can be made convertible on the capital account.
"Sledgehammer-type convertibility may not help. We should have it in a phased manner," Raghuraman said.

The conditions spelt out in the report included an average inflation rate of three to five percent for the three-year period until 2000, and a reduction in the fiscal deficit as a percentage of gross domestic product (GDP) to 3.5 percent by 1999/2000 (April-March).
The industry leaders welcomed the report and said it signalled the government's intention to move towards a free-market regime.
The Confederation of Indian Industry said it was an example of government action to improve the climate to make business and industry free of old and outdated practices and regulations.
"Three years are good enough to make a changeover to full convertibility," Raghuraman said.
The rupee was made convertible on the current account of the balance of payments in August 1994. Current account transactions refer to transactions in goods and services.
Capital account convertibility implies the right to transact in financial assets with foreign countries without restrictions.

"Although the fundamentals of the economy are strong, it needs to be further strengthened before full convertibility," said Y.P. Srivastava, deputy secretary general of Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FICCI).
"We should also have comfortable foreign exchange reserves," he added.
Industry leaders said the move towards capital account convertibility would depend on macroeconomic stability.
"We have to control fiscal deficit, inflation and current account deficit on balance of payments," Raghuraman said.
India aims to slash fiscal deficit to 4.0 percent of GDP in 1997/98 (April-March) compared to 5.0 percent in the previous year.
"We still have lot of restrictions on exports and imports. This affects capital inflow," Shashanka Bhide, an economic at National Council of Applied Economic Research (NCAER), told Reuters.
"What remains to be done is to remove the restrictions in the trade regime," he said, when asked about the obstacles to full covertibility.
